name: Magnus force
seoDesc: Magnus force: work out fluid from the length and the rotational speed. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Magnus force calculator the length, the rotational speed, the vortex strength and the free stream velocity and it returns fluid. It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Magnus force calculator work?
sections.html:
The Magnus force calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports fluid in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the length (ℓ), the rotational speed (vr), the vortex strength (G) and the free stream velocity (vfrₑₑ).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters per second. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in square meters per second. The unit chip switches it to any of the 9 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters per second. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in newtons. The unit chip switches it to any of the 16 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Magnus force calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Fluid=density (ρ)
Radius (r)=(1 ÷ 2) × vortex strength (G) ÷ (PI × rotational speed (vr))
Radius (r)=(1 ÷ 2) × rotational speed (vr) ÷ (PI × rate of rotation (f))
Density (ρ)=magnus force ÷ (free stream velocity (vfrₑₑ) × length (ℓ) × vortex strength (G))
Rate of rotation (f)=(1 ÷ 2) × angular velocity (ω) ÷ PI

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — Fluid set to Air — it reports Density (ρ) = 1.225 kg/m³.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Density (ρ) = 1.225 kg/m³ should be roughly the size you expected from Fluid set to Air.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.
  • Shown in meters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in kilograms per cubic meter, and convertible to any of the 9 units on that chip.
  • Shown in radians per second, and convertible to any of the 3 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Rotational speed, opening in radians per second
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Viscosity – kinematic, opening in square meters per second
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Force, opening in newtons

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Magnus force calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the length, the rotational speed and the vortex strength — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Magnus force calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns fluid, derived from the length, the rotational speed and the vortex strength. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Magnus force calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length, the rotational speed, the vortex strength and the free stream velocity, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter radius (r) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Radius (r) opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Density (ρ) = 1.225 kg/m³. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Magnus force calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
